We recall (see, for instance, [1, p. 19]) that the lattice generated by vectors al, a 2 . . . , am in a Euclidean
space V is the collection L of all vectors of V of the shape

                                       ~lal   -[- ot2a2 -[- ' ' - q- Otrnam,   oti E Z.

Henceforth we use function notations and denote this lattice L b y / : ( a l , . . . , a m ) . Clearly, the members
of a lattice form an additive subgroup of the group of all vectors of V.
    Lattices appear in various fields of mathematics such as number theory, group theory (classification
of simple finite groups and study of crystallographic groups), coding theory, the classical problem of
sphere packing, etc. (see [2]). Lattices seem to appear for the first time in number theory, namely, in
the section of it which is called "geometry of numbers" and whose foundations were laid in the works
by Hermit, Minkowski, VoronoY, et al. (see [1; 3, Chapter 2]).
    It is well known [4, p. 223] that every subspace U of a finite-dimensional Euclidean space V
possesses an orthonormal basis. The natural question arises: given a finite-dimensional Euclidean
space V and a lattice L in V, under wha:t conditions does L possess an orthogonal basis in the sense
of the standard inner product in V? The present article addresses this question.
    Fix some orthonormai basis for V and consider the coordinates of all vectors with respect to this
basis. Call a lattice L in V rational (integer) if all vectors in L have rational (integer) coordinates.
In this article we prove that construction of an orthogonal basis for a rational lattice reduces to
construction of an orthogonal basis for some integer lattice. Afterwards we give a sufficient condition
for existence of an orthogonal basis for an integer lattice. Next in w2 we examine two-dimensional
integer lattices in more detail and give a criterion for existence of an orthogonal basis. In w3 we study
complete two-dimensional lattices and give a simpler criterion for existence of an orthogonal basis
which is based on construction of some canonical basis for a two-dimensional integer lattice. In w4
we use the results obtained to give a partial answer to Problem 9.45 in [5]: "Let a be a vector in
R n with rational components and let S ( a ) = { k a + b [ k E Z, and b E Z'~}. Find necessary and
sufficient conditions in terms of the components of a for S ( a ) to have an orthogonal basis in the sense
of the standard inner product of Rn." We give a sufficient condition for existence of an orthogonal
basis for S ( a ) in the case of n > 1, and obtain a sought criterion for n = 2.
    The author is grateful to the participants of the seminar "Evariste Galois" who have listened
the proofs and made a number of useful suggestions and remarks.
    The author is grateful to the referee for fruitful remarks.

By an elementary transformation of a matrix we always mean an integer transformation of the rows of
the matrix, i.e., multiplication of some row by - 1 , as well as multiplication of some row by an integer
and addition to another row. If integer vectors a l , . . . , a m generate a lattice L then we can find
a basis for this lattice (there exists a basis since L is a torsion-free finitely-generated abelian group).
Furthermore, with each system of generators a l , . . . , am of L we can associate the matrix A = (ai) ,
i = 1 , . . . ,rn, j = 1 , . . . ,n, whose rows are the coordinates of the vectors a l , . . . ,am. The converse
is true as well: each integer matrix in Mm,n(Z) corresponds to the lattice generated by the rows of
the matrix. Using Euclid's algorithm and applying elementary transformations to the m a t r i x A, we
can reduce it to triangular form [8, p. 29]. Then the nonzero rows of the resultant matrix constitute
a ladder basis for the lattice L:

     L e m m a 1. Let F be the Gram matrix of some basis t'or an integer m-dimensional lattice L.
The lattice L possesses an orthogonal basis if and only if there exists a m a t r i x T E GLm(Z) such that
T F T t is a diagonal matrix.
    We now demonstrate that construction of an orthogonal basis for a rational lattice reduces to
construction of an orthogonal basis for some integer lattice. More precisely, the following assertion
holds.
    L e m m a 2. For every rational lattice L, there exists an isomorphic integer lattice M such that L
possesses an orthogonal basis if and only if M possesses an orthogonal basis.

        We formulate a sufficient condition for existence of an orthogonal basis for an integer lattice.
        L e m m a 3. If, in a ladder basis C l , . . . , Cr, r > 2, for an integer lattice L, the orthogonal pro-
jection of the vector ci, i = 1 , . . . , r -         1, onto the support s u p p ( c i + l , . . . , c r ) lies in the sublattice

an orthogonal basis for L. The proof of the lemma is over.
     We shall see below that the condition of the lemma is sufficient but not necessary for existence of
an orthogonal basis.

    We recall that a lattice L in a vector space V is said to be complete if its dimension equals
the dimension of V. In this section we give a simpler criterion of existence of an orthogonal basis for
a complete two-dimensionai lattice L which leans upon the comparison between the bases for L and
the integer matrices in M2(Z).
    Suppose that integer vectors al = (a~, a 2) and a2 = (a~, a 2) form a basis for a complete lattice L.
Then we can consider the matrix


as the matrix of a linear transformation taking the lattice Zel ~ Ze2 onto the lattice L. To another
basis for L, there corresponds the matrix TA, where T is a matrix in GL2(Z). If the matrix TA
corresponds to an orthogonal basis for L then the matrix TA(TA) t is diagonal. The matrices satisfying
this condition are described in the following obvious lemma.
    L e m m a 7. Let B E M2(Z) be a matrix such that B B t is diagonal Then B has the shape

In particular, if there exists a matrix T E GL2(Z) such that TA corresponds to an orthogonal basis
then, without loss of generality, we may assume that det T = 1. "

                                                                                                         1075
     C o r o l l a r y . Let L be a complete two-dimensional lattice with the following matrix of a standard
basis:                          /

                         A=

/[ a, b, and c satisfy at least one of the conditions
     (1) c is free of squares and has as prime factors only numbers of the shape 4k + 3;
     (2) a > c
then the lattice L does not possess an orthogonal basis.
     PROOF. It is well known (see, for instance, [10, p. 116]) that an integer N is representable as
the sum of two squares if and only if every prime factor of N of the shape 4k + 3 enters into N with
an even power. Hence, if c is free of squares and only has prime factors of t h e shape 4k + 3, then c
cannot be represented as c = fig1 (f~2Xl  2 + g0Yl),
                                               2 2 where the integers fl, gl, fo, go, xl, and yl satisfy
condition (1) of Theorem 2.
     Suppose that condition (2) of the corollary is satisfied, but the lattice L nevertheless possesses
an orthogonal basis. By Theorem 2, then there are positive integers f0 and go such that a = logo
and there are integers f,, gl, xl, and yl such that c = fig1 (f~z 2 + g2y2). T h e obvious inequality
]-2 + g02 + (f0 - g0)2 > 0 readily implies that ]-2 + gg > logo. Since c > ]-2 + g2, it follows that c > a,
contradicting the supposition. The proof of the corollary is over.
